name: Model Extraction Defence Testing
description: Model extraction defence testing checks whether a model offered through a query interface, such as a prediction API, can be copied by someone who can only send it inputs and read its outputs. The tester plays the attacker, spends a fixed query budget on the protected interface, then uses the answers to train a surrogate model (a copy trained on the answers) or to solve for the model's parameters, and compares the copy with the original. Fidelity is usually measured as the share of inputs on which the copy agrees with the original, together with how many queries that took. The same attack is run with and without each defence, such as limiting queries, rounding or removing confidence scores, or adding noise to outputs, to show how much each defence raises the attacker's cost. The tester also measures the effect on legitimate users, for example accuracy or response time.

example_use_cases.description: Testing protections for a proprietary fraud detection API to ensure competitors cannot recreate the model's decision boundaries through systematic querying, by simulating extraction attacks using query budgets, active learning strategies, and substitute model training.

Evaluating whether rate limiting and output obfuscation for an automated essay grading API prevent competitors from extracting the scoring model through systematic submission of probe essays designed to reverse-engineer grading criteria.

A transport authority sells access to a traffic-prediction API and rounds its forecasts to deter copying. It runs extraction attacks against rounded and unrounded versions to see how much rounding makes a surrogate lose fidelity, then checks that the rounded forecasts remain accurate enough for urban planners.

limitations.description: A defence is tested only against the attacks the tester thinks to run, and attackers adapt. A 2024 attack recovered part of production language models through log-probability and logit-bias options that designers had treated as harmless, so passing a test is not a guarantee of protection.

Defences that perturb or hide outputs can reduce utility for legitimate users, and the acceptable loss depends on the application. The test has to measure legitimate accuracy and latency as well as extraction fidelity, or it will reward defences that quietly break the service.

It is hard to tell legitimate high-volume use from extraction, so query limits and detection can block valid users. Published stateful detection defences have themselves been bypassed, so a detector that passes a test may still fail against an adaptive attacker.

Results depend on what the simulated attacker is assumed to know, such as the model type, the training-data distribution, and whether the API returns confidence scores or accepts partial inputs. Testing against a weak assumed attacker overstates protection.

There is no agreed threshold for how much copying fidelity is acceptable, and a fidelity figure depends on the query budget and the measure used. Results are therefore hard to compare across models and defences, and the pass mark is a judgement.

resources.title: Stealing Machine Learning Models via Prediction APIs
resources.abstract: Machine learning (ML) models may be deemed confidential due to their sensitive training data, commercial value, or use in security applications. Increasingly often, confidential ML models are being deployed with publicly accessible query interfaces. ML-as-a-service ("predictive analytics") systems are an example: Some allow users to train models on potentially sensitive data and charge others for access on a pay-per-query basis. The tension between model confidentiality and public access motivates our investigation of model extraction attacks. In such attacks, an adversary with black-box access, but no prior knowledge of an ML model's parameters or training data, aims to duplicate the functionality of (i.e., "steal") the model. Unlike in classical learning theory settings, ML-as-a-service offerings may accept partial feature vectors as inputs and include confidence values with predictions. Given these practices, we show simple, efficient attacks that extract target ML models with near-perfect fidelity for popular model classes including logistic regression, neural networks, and decision trees. We demonstrate these attacks against the online services of BigML and Amazon Machine Learning. We further show that the natural countermeasure of omitting confidence values from model outputs still admits potentially harmful model extraction attacks. Our results highlight the need for careful ML model deployment and new model extraction countermeasures.

resources.title: Stealing Part of a Production Language Model
resources.abstract: We introduce the first model-stealing attack that extracts precise, nontrivial information from black-box production language models like OpenAI's ChatGPT or Google's PaLM-2. Specifically, our attack recovers the embedding projection layer (up to symmetries) of a transformer model, given typical API access. For under \$20 USD, our attack extracts the entire projection matrix of OpenAI's Ada and Babbage language models. We thereby confirm, for the first time, that these black-box models have a hidden dimension of 1024 and 2048, respectively. We also recover the exact hidden dimension size of the gpt-3.5-turbo model, and estimate it would cost under $2,000 in queries to recover the entire projection matrix. We conclude with potential defenses and mitigations, and discuss the implications of possible future work that could extend our attack.

sample_claims.text: Under the documented query budget, the fraud API's output restriction reduced extracted-model agreement compared with the unrestricted baseline.
The essay-scoring API evaluation reports extraction success and rejection of legitimate requests for the tested rate-limit settings.

A surrogate model trained on answers from the traffic-prediction API within the permitted query budget agrees with the production model on no more than an agreed share of held-out inputs, while the forecasts stay accurate enough for planners
The prediction API returns only the output fields its legitimate users need, so extraction attacks that depend on confidence scores or partial inputs do not succeed
